etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English outlawe, outlagh, utlaȝe, from Old English ūtlaga (“outlaw”), borrowed from Old Norse útlagi (“outlaw, fugitive”), equivalent to out- +‎ law. Cognate with Icelandic útlagi (“outlaw”).

definitions.definition: (history) A criminal who is excluded from normal legal rights; one who can be killed at will without legal penalty.
A person who operates outside established norms.
(humorous) An in-law: a relative by marriage.
(humorous) One who would be an in-law except that the  marriage-like relationship is unofficial.
(slang) A prostitute who works alone, without a pimp.

quote.text: Without a pimp, she was an "outlaw," likely to be harassed, or threatened with assault or robbery on the street.

quote.citation: 2010, Lawrence Block, Eight Million Ways To Die:
quote.text: She was an outlaw. Chance is doing some double-checking to see if she had a pimp nobody knew about, but it doesn't look likely.

quote.citation: 2016 August 15, “'Zombie knives' ban to come into force”, in BBC News‎[1]:
quote.text: The legal change in England and Wales will outlaw selling, manufacturing, renting or importing zombie knives.

definitions.definition: To make or declare (a person) an outlaw.

quote.citation: 1880, John Sephton, transl., The Saga of Erik the Red:
quote.text: Eirik and his people were outlawed at Thorsnes Thing.

definitions.definition: To remove from legal jurisdiction or enforcement.

quote.citation: a. 1662 (date written), Thomas Fuller, The History of the Worthies of England, London:  […]  J[ohn] G[rismond,] W[illiam] L[eybourne] and W[illiam] G[odbid], published 1662, →OCLC:
quote.text: our English common law was outlawed in those parts.
